analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced January 21, 2015 with 37 Republican sponsors, it sat in the Senate Homeland Security committee for the rest of the Congress, which ended January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the way Washington issues 'major' rules — ones costing the economy $100 million or more, raising prices significantly, or hurting competition or jobs. No such rule could take effect unless both chambers of Congress passed a resolution approving it; if they did not act within 70 days, the rule would die automatically. In effect, any single chamber could kill a major regulation just by doing nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies in heavily regulated industries — energy, mining, chemicals, manufacturing, finance — would gain a powerful tool. Under the bill, a major rule they oppose could be stopped indefinitely if either chamber simply declined to act, since the rule would be 'deemed not to be approved' when the clock ran out. That gives opponents of a rule a veto without ever having to vote against it on the record.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Regulated industries facing costly new rules

how_it_helps.text: Any rule the budget office finds likely to cost the economy $100 million or more a year, raise costs or prices significantly, or hurt competition, employment, or investment would be classified as 'major' and could not take effect until Congress passed a joint resolution of approval.
If no approval resolution were enacted within 70 session or legislative days after the agency submits its report, the rule would be deemed not approved and would never take effect.

A President could let a major rule take effect temporarily — for one 90-day period — only for an imminent health or safety threat, criminal law enforcement, national security, or an international trade agreement.
Approval resolutions could not be amended at any stage, and the bill sets fast-track procedures with limited debate and guaranteed votes in each chamber.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal rules for clean air and water, workplace and food safety, and consumer financial protection. Under the bill, every major protection in those areas would need positive action from both chambers of Congress — and any of the four could be stopped by inaction in one.
analysis.who_pays_short: People protected by federal safety and environmental rules

drawbacks.text: The most common criticism of this approach is that a 70-day deadline with automatic death makes major protections hostage to gridlock: whichever chamber opposes a rule can kill it by doing nothing, so the strongest rules face the greatest risk.
Even in a genuine emergency, a major rule could only take effect for a single 90-day period without congressional approval, which could leave dangerous gaps if Congress fails to act.

Supporters' strongest good-faith point is real: Congress has delegated broad lawmaking power to agencies and rarely votes on the specific rules that carry the force of law, and this bill would force a recorded vote. An honest supporter must also acknowledge the cost — Congress historically approves very few things on a fast clock, so the practical effect would be to stop most major rules rather than review them.
The bill explicitly exempts monetary policy rules from the Federal Reserve and exempts rules on hunting, fishing, and camping from the approval process entirely.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is genuine — Congress should own the laws it delegates — but the design converts that idea into a unilateral kill switch. Because inaction in a single chamber kills a rule, the realistic result is not careful review of each rule but a near-blanket stop on major regulation, and the largest costs would fall on the public protections those rules provide.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee took no further action, and the Congress ended in January 2017 with no vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on January 21, 2015, joined by 36 Republican cosponsors; every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day, which was its last recorded action.
No committee vote, floor vote, or other action occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system stayed in place: federal agencies could keep issuing major rules without a congressional vote, and industries that wanted a congressional veto over regulation did not get one. Companies already operating under pending major rules were better off than under the bill; the public's health, safety, and environmental protections remained as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies kept authority; industries got no veto

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 21, 2015 and argued it would force Congress to vote on the major rules it delegates to agencies.

for.name: 36 of 54 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican.

against.name: Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on January 21, 2015 and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the Senate never voted on the bill.

industries.industry: Heavily regulated industries (energy, mining, chemicals, manufacturing, finance)
industries.note: These industries would gain the practical ability to block any major rule by getting one chamber to sit on its hands for 70 days, since unapproved rules die automatically. The gain comes directly at the expense of the public protections those rules enforce.

Agencies would lose the power to put major rules into effect on their own authority; their work would become contingent on affirmative congressional approval. Their loss is the public's gain only to the extent Congress actually acts rather than stalls.

The bill transfers approval power over major rules from the executive branch to Congress, giving every incumbent legislator leverage over regulatory outcomes. That power could be used for accountability or for blocking, and the bill's structure rewards blocking.
